paper_a.title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space

paper_b.title: GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation

metadata.description: Both papers learn dense word embeddings that encode linear semantic and syntactic regularities (the 'king - man + woman = queen' property), but via competing frameworks. word2vec (paper A) is a local-context, on-line, log-linear neural predictor (CBOW / Skip-gram) that performs implicit factorization of a shifted PMI matrix; GloVe (paper B) is a global, weighted least-squares explicit factorization of the log word-word co-occurrence matrix. They share the analogy task, the cosine-arithmetic solver, AdaGrad optimization and (cited) skip-gram baselines, but diverge sharply on objective, training signal (predict-vs-fit) and complexity analysis (hidden-layer cost vs harmonic-number / power-law).

matches.explanation: Both pose the unsupervised problem of learning real-valued word vectors that capture semantic/syntactic regularities. Paper A's framing emphasises a fixed training-time budget while choosing architecture, $D$, vocab and corpus size; paper B's framing emphasises that linear vector arithmetic should encode analogies. Same underlying problem, different optimisation criteria, hence analogous.

The Mikolov word-analogy task is the same object on both sides: paper A defines it (DP208.5) and supplies the $vector(b)-vector(a)+vector(c)$ + cosine-nearest solver (AP208.6); paper B reuses it as cited evaluation (ProbP209.2) — with the same vector-arithmetic, cosine-similarity decision rule. PDF-fallback caveat noted but identity is unambiguous because B explicitly cites Mikolov 2013a.

Paper A's Semantic-Syntactic Word Relationship test set (8869 semantic + 10675 syntactic = 19544 questions) is exactly the dataset that paper B's analogy task (19544 questions, semantic + syntactic split) evaluates. Same benchmark; B references it as external.

Both nodes are the CBOW model: a log-linear / single-layer predictor of a target word from the average of its context vectors. Paper A is the originator (AP208.3, origin paper); paper B cites it (AP209.3, origin external). Names and types align; statements describe the same architecture.

Both are the Skip-gram model: predict surrounding words from the current word via a log-linear softmax. Paper A introduces it (AP208.4, origin paper); paper B cites it (AP209.2, origin external) and even compares against it head-to-head in ExP209.6. Same algorithm.

Composite parent-with-steps comparison of the two papers' core training algorithms. Skip-gram (A) does on-line per-token SGD on (input,output) pairs sampled by random window radius and updates via hierarchical-softmax backprop (ASP208.5-8). GloVe (B) instead pre-builds a global co-occurrence matrix $X$, initialises word/context/bias parameters, and runs AdaGrad over nonzero entries minimising the weighted log-squared-error cost, returning $W+\tilde W$ (ASP209.1-4). Both end up factorising co-occurrence statistics, but the step DAGs reveal the predict-vs-fit divide that defines the CF relationship.

The Bengio NNLM appears in paper A as a cited baseline architecture central to the complexity comparison; paper B does not represent it explicitly (it groups all neural local-context methods under skip-gram/CBOW/ivLBL).
RNNLM is a paper-A baseline (cited from Mikolov 2010) with no counterpart in paper B's representation set.

Paper A uses DistBelief asynchronous mini-batch SGD with Adagrad as its parallel training framework (AP208.5); paper B uses AdaGrad as its optimiser (AP209.6). Both lean on Duchi et al. 2011's adaptive learning rate, but A's node bundles the distributed-training infrastructure while B's is single-machine AdaGrad. They overlap in the optimiser but differ in scope; medium confidence.

Hierarchical softmax with a Huffman binary tree is central to word2vec's efficient training. GloVe avoids softmax entirely (it does explicit log-count regression), so this construction has no GloVe counterpart.

Both papers analyse training-time complexity, but with sharply different machinery. Paper A defines complexity as parameter accesses ($O = E\,T\,Q$) and tabulates per-example $Q$ for NNLM, RNNLM, CBOW, Skip-gram. Paper B models co-occurrences as a power law $X_{ij}=k/r_{ij}^{\alpha}$ and bounds the number of nonzeros via the generalized harmonic number ($|X|=O(|C|^{0.8})$ at $\alpha=1.25$). Both target 'how does cost scale with corpus / vocabulary?'; both are normative complexity claims; but the underlying analyses are not directly translatable - this is precisely the CF-flavoured contrast.

'Hidden layer dominates NNLM cost' is paper A's motivating claim for moving to log-linear shallow models. Paper B never discusses neural hidden-layer costs (its complexity analysis is co-occurrence-matrix based).

The 'multiple degrees of similarity' / linear-arithmetic property ($King-Man+Woman \approx Queen$) is the same observation in both papers. A states it as a claim about word vectors; B builds it into the problem statement and gives the king/queen/man/woman example (ExP209.2).

'Joint scaling of D and T' is an empirical claim from paper A's CBOW dimensionality-vs-data sweep with no equivalent in paper B (B varies $d$ and corpus but as separate ablations, not as a joint-scaling principle).

Paper A claims Skip-gram beats CBOW/NNLM/RNNLM on semantic analogies. Paper B's same-data comparison (ExP209.6) instead claims GloVe beats CBOW and Skip-gram on the same task. Both are head-to-head architecture-comparison claims on the analogy benchmark, but the winners disagree - emblematic of the CF relationship. Analogous in role.
'1-epoch on 2x data matches 3-epoch on original' is a paper-A specific empirical recommendation; paper B fixes a per-iteration AdaGrad schedule and does not study epoch-count tradeoffs.
DistBelief 6B-word Skip-gram state-of-the-art result is paper-A specific.

MSR Sentence Completion Challenge (ProbP208.2), the Skip-gram scoring algorithm for it (AP208.7) and the Skip-gram+RNNLM SOTA claim (ClP208.7) form a paper-A specific application cluster absent from paper B.
The word-word co-occurrence matrix $X$ is GloVe's central object. word2vec implicitly factorises a related matrix but never names or builds $X$ explicitly, so paper A has no corresponding node.
Row sum $X_i$ and conditional probability $P_{ij}=X_{ij}/X_i$ are GloVe-specific; word2vec does not define them.

GloVe maintains separate word ($w$) and context ($\tilde w$) vectors and combines them as $W+\tilde W$. word2vec also has input/output embedding matrices but does not name them as a paired construct in this extraction; emit as none on B-side to flag the asymmetry.
The co-occurrence probability ratio $P_{ik}/P_{jk}$ is GloVe's key motivating quantity (used to discriminate target words via probe $k$); word2vec's framework has no analogue.
GloVe's bounded power-law weighting function $f(x)$ is specific to its weighted least-squares objective; word2vec uses no such weighting.

GloVe's derivation chain $F(w_i,w_j,\tilde w_k)=P_{ik}/P_{jk}$ -> vector-difference -> dot-product -> homomorphism -> $F=\exp$ -> $w_i^T\tilde w_k+b_i+\tilde b_k=\log X_{ik}$ -> weighted-LS cost is GloVe-specific machinery with no word2vec counterpart. Emitted as a single composite none on the B-only side.

GloVe's recasting of the global skip-gram objective as a weighted cross-entropy and its proof of equivalence (up to bias terms) to the GloVe weighted log-squared-error cost. This is a paper-B specific bridge claim - it argues that word2vec is a special / suboptimal case of B's framework. Could be tagged as PR-flavour evidence; but as a node it has no matching A-side construct.

Derivation of the GloVe log model from the desiderata (vector-difference -> dot-product -> homomorphism -> $F=\exp$) is paper-B specific machinery. word2vec contains no analogous proof - its log-linear models are introduced operationally rather than derived axiomatically.

Derivation of GloVe's complexity bound $|X|=O(|C|^{1/\alpha})$ via the generalized harmonic number expansion is paper-B specific. Paper A's complexity discussion is by direct per-example $Q$ counts, not via an asymptotic proof.
LSA and the SVD/SVD-S/SVD-L baselines are GloVe-side baselines from the matrix-factorisation tradition; word2vec does not include them in its baseline set.

Word-similarity (Spearman correlation on WS353/MC/RG/SCWS/RW) and CoNLL-2003 NER are GloVe-side evaluation tasks; word2vec evaluates only on the Mikolov analogy and MSR Sentence Completion benchmarks.
